p: The letter names Paul. Most critical scholars think a follower wrote it in his name; others defend Paul.
b: The letter opens with Paul's name, and by the late second century the church quoted it as his: Irenaeus (Against Heresies 3.3.4) cites 3:10 with the words "as Paul also says". Since the 1800s most critical scholars have held that 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy and Titus were written together by a follower of Paul after his death; a strong minority defends Paul, often with a secretary. The arguments, and how Marcion and the early writers treated the three letters, are set out once, on the topic page The Pastoral Letters. This Plain follows the text and calls the writer Paul, as the letter does. The book page gives the points that touch Titus alone: the journey to Crete that Acts does not record, and the winter at Nicopolis (3:12).

t: "A slave of God": a title found only here
p: Paul usually calls himself a slave "of Christ Jesus." Only here is he "a slave of God."
b: The Greek doulos means a slave, a person owned by another, and this site renders it "slave" everywhere, as in Romans 1:1, "a slave of Christ Jesus." Many English Bibles soften it to "servant", but in the Roman world a slave belonged to a master and carried out his will, and a slave of a powerful house could carry real authority in his master's name. The phrase "slave of God" also echoes the Old Testament title of Moses, David and the prophets, "the servant of the LORD." In Paul's letters it appears only here. The letter will speak of slaves in Cretan households in 2:9-10, and they are called by the same word, doulos, that Paul uses of himself here.

a: for the faith of God's chosen ones
t: For their faith, or in keeping with it?
p: The little word kata can mean "for the sake of" or "in line with" the faith of God's people.
b: The Greek says Paul is an apostle kata pistin eklekton theou. Kata usually means "according to", so the phrase may mean that Paul's work matches the faith God's people already have. But it can also give a goal, "for the sake of" their faith: Paul was sent to bring God's chosen ones to faith and to knowledge of the truth. The Plain's "for" keeps the second reading, which the next phrase supports: "for the knowledge of the truth" also names something to be reached. The "chosen ones" are God's people, as in Romans 8:33.
orig: κατὰ πίστιν ἐκλεκτῶν θεοῦ (kata pistin eklektōn theou)

t: Godliness: the Pastorals' word for faith lived out
p: Eusebeia, a common Greek virtue, is one of the key words of the three Pastoral Letters.
b: The Greek eusebeia was the ordinary word for piety: proper reverence toward the gods, toward parents and toward one's city. Paul's undisputed letters never use it, but the Pastorals use it often (1 Timothy 2:2; 4:7-8; 6:6; 2 Timothy 3:5), and Titus uses it here and in 2:12, "in a godly way." It means reverence for God that shows in how a person lives. The truth Paul preaches "goes with" it: right belief and right living belong together. That is the theme of the whole letter, which ends each section with good works (1:16; 2:14; 3:8, 14). The opposite, asebeia "ungodliness", comes in 2:12.

a: The God who does not lie
p: One Greek word, apseudes, "without lies." It sets up the sharp contrast with the Cretan liars of 1:12.
b: The adjective apseudēs means "free of falsehood" and appears only here in the New Testament. It stands at the start of a letter that will quote the line "Cretans are always liars" (1:12). The contrast looks deliberate: God, who does not lie, against a people famous for lying and teachers who "lead minds astray" (1:10). The idea is old: "God is not a man, that he should lie" (Numbers 23:19), and Hebrews 6:18 says it is impossible for God to lie. A promise from such a God is the ground of the "hope of eternal life."

a: before the long ages of time
p: The Greek says the promise came "before times of the ages." It may mean before creation or long ago.
b: The phrase pro chronōn aiōniōn means literally "before times eternal" or "before the times of the ages." Two readings are common. Some take it as before the world began, so that God's promise of life was made in eternity, within God himself (compare 2 Timothy 1:9, where grace was given "before the long ages of time", the same Greek phrase, rendered the same way here). Others take it as "long ages ago", the promises given through Abraham and the prophets. Romans 1:2 says that "God promised this good news ahead of time through his prophets", which supports the second; the parallel in 2 Timothy 1:9 supports the first. The Plain keeps the time words so both remain possible.

a: he brought his word into the open
p: The pattern of a promise kept quiet for ages and then made public is one of Paul's favorites.
b: The verb phaneroō means "make visible." Romans ends with the same pattern: a mystery kept silent for long ages, "but now brought into the open" (Romans 16:26), and Ephesians 3:5 and Colossians 1:26 say the same. Here what comes into the open is God's "word", the message about Christ, and it happens through preaching. The phrase "at the times he set" (literally "at its own times", plural) says God picked the moment, as in Galatians 4:4, "when the time had come to its fullness."

p: The Greek kerygma is a herald's announcement. Later scholars use it for the core message of the first Christians.
b: The noun kērygma comes from kēryx, a herald who announced a ruler's news in the town square. It can mean the act of proclaiming or the message proclaimed. Paul uses it for his preaching of Christ crucified (1 Corinthians 1:21; 2:4; 15:14). Modern scholars borrowed the word to name the basic outline of the early Christian message: Jesus died for our sins, was raised, and will come again. Titus contains a short summary of that kind in 2:11-14 and another in 3:4-7.

p: Titus calls God "our Savior" three times and Jesus "our Savior" three times, side by side.
b: The title sōtēr, "savior", was common in the Greek world for gods who rescued and for kings and emperors who claimed to bring peace and safety. In Titus the title passes back and forth: God is "our Savior" in 1:3, 2:10 and 3:4, and Christ Jesus is "our Savior" in 1:4, 2:13 and 3:6. Each pair stands close together (1:3 and 1:4; 2:10 and 2:13; 3:4 and 3:6). The writer does not explain how the two relate, but he puts them in the same place, which matters for the reading of 2:13. In the Old Testament "savior" is a title of the LORD (Isaiah 43:11).

p: Titus is never named in Acts, but Paul's other letters show him as a trusted partner sent on hard tasks.
b: Titus was a Greek. Paul took him to Jerusalem, and "not even he was made to get circumcised" (Galatians 2:3), so he was a living test case in the argument over the law. Later he carried Paul's hard words to Corinth and came back with good news: "God ... comforted us by the arrival of Titus" (2 Corinthians 7:6). He organized the collection there, and Paul calls him "my partner and my fellow worker" (2 Corinthians 8:23). This letter finds him on Crete, and 2 Timothy 4:10 sends him to Dalmatia. Acts never mentions him, which is one of the puzzles of his story.
r: Galatians 2:1-3; 2 Corinthians 2:13; 2 Corinthians 7:6; 2 Corinthians 8:6; 2 Corinthians 8:23; 2 Corinthians 12:18; 2 Timothy 4:10

p: Gnesios means a child born in wedlock, the true heir. Paul may mean he brought Titus to faith.
b: The word gnēsios was used of a legitimate child, born to the family and with a right to inherit, as opposed to an illegitimate one. Paul uses the same phrase for Timothy (1 Timothy 1:2). It may mean that Titus came to faith through Paul, or simply that Titus is Paul's true representative, the one who carries his authority on Crete. The phrase "in the faith we hold in common" adds that the bond between the Jew Paul and the Greek Titus rests on the faith they share, not on birth.

p: Acts mentions Crete only as a stop on Paul's voyage as a prisoner. This mission is not in Acts.
b: In Acts, Paul sees Crete only from a ship under guard: they "ran down along the sheltered side of Crete" (Acts 27:7), put in at Fair Havens, and were driven off by a storm (Acts 27:13-21). There was no time for a mission. So a stay on Crete with Titus does not fit the story of Acts. Those who hold that Paul wrote Titus place the visit after Acts ends, when they think Paul was set free and traveled again. Those who hold that a follower wrote it see here one sign of a setting made for the letter. There were believers from Crete from the start, though: "Some are Cretans and Arabs" (Acts 2:11), at Pentecost.

p: Crete had many towns. Titus was to see that each Christian group had its own elders.
b: The Greek kata polin means "town by town" or "in each city." Crete was a large island with many towns, so the church was scattered in small groups. "Elders" (presbyteroi, the word behind English "presbyter" and "priest") were the senior men who led Jewish communities and then the churches (Acts 14:23: "They chose elders for them in each church"). The verb kathistēmi means "set in place, appoint": Titus acts by Paul's instruction. Calvin argued that Titus presided over the choosing, "as moderator", and did not pick men alone; others read the verse as appointment by an apostle's delegate. The card on the chapter page sets out the churches' readings.
orig: καταστήσῃς κατὰ πόλιν πρεσβυτέρους (katastēsēs kata polin presbyterous)

t: "The husband of one wife": five readings
p: The Greek is literally "a man of one woman." Churches have read it at least five ways.
b: The phrase mias gynaikos anēr is also in 1 Timothy 3:2, 12, and 1 Timothy 5:9 has its mirror, "the wife of one husband." This Plain keeps it literal so that every reading stays open: (1) not a polygamist; (2) not remarried after a divorce; (3) never married a second time at all, even after a wife's death; (4) faithful to his wife, a "one-woman man"; (5) a married man, not single. Chrysostom took it to show that marriage is honorable, "that a married man might ascend the holy throne", and also to exclude a man who had married a second time. Many modern Protestant readers take it as faithfulness. The mirror phrase for widows in 1 Timothy 5:9 makes polygamy alone an unlikely meaning, since women did not have several husbands at once.

p: Tekna pista can mean children who are believers, or children who are faithful and well behaved.
b: The Greek pistos means "faithful, trustworthy" and also "believing." So tekna pista can be "children who believe" or "children who can be trusted." The difference is large in practice: on the first reading a man whose grown child has left the faith could not be an elder; on the second, the point is a well-ordered household, as in 1 Timothy 3:4, where the overseer keeps his children under control. The rest of the verse, "not open to a charge of wild living or of being unruly", is about conduct, which favors the second. Elsewhere in Titus pistos means "trustworthy" (1:9; 3:8). Chrysostom drew the lesson that a man who cannot teach his own children cannot teach the church. The Plain's "faithful" keeps both meanings.

p: The same root describes the younger son in Luke 15:13, who scattered his estate, "living a wasteful life."
b: The noun asōtia means a reckless, wasteful life, money and self thrown away. Its adverb describes the younger son in the parable who scattered his share of the estate (Luke 15:13), and Ephesians 5:18 uses the noun of drunkenness. A leader's grown children who were known around town for parties and debts would bring shame on him and on the church in a culture where a household's reputation was public.

t: Elder and overseer: one office here
p: The verse switches from "elders" (1:5) to "the overseer" without a break. Here they seem to be the same people.
b: The Greek episkopos means "overseer", and it is the word behind English "bishop" (through Latin episcopus). Verse 5 speaks of appointing elders; verse 7 gives the reason with "for" and speaks of "the overseer." So most readers, ancient and modern, take the two words as names for the same leaders, as in Acts 20:17, 28, where the Ephesian "elders" are told the Holy Spirit made them "overseers." Chrysostom said that in this passage "he is speaking of Bishops" when he says elders; Calvin said the passage "plainly shows that there is no distinction between a presbyter and a bishop." Churches with bishops answer that the words had not yet settled into the later ranks. See the card on the chapter page.

p: An oikonomos ran a large household for its owner, often as a trusted slave.
b: The oikonomos managed a rich man's house: he handled the money, the stores and the other slaves, and answered to the owner. Jesus' parables use the word (Luke 12:42; 16:1-8), and Paul calls himself and Apollos "stewards of God's mysteries" (1 Corinthians 4:1). The image explains the list that follows. The church is God's household (1 Timothy 3:15), so its manager must be honest with money ("not greedy for shameful profit"), in control of himself, and trusted by the owner. The word oikonomia (Ephesians 1:10, "plan") comes from the same root.

p: The word describes a man always at his wine, and often the quarrels that come with it.
b: The Greek paroinos is literally "by the wine": someone who sits long at drink and grows rough with it. It is the same word in 1 Timothy 3:3. The next word, plēktēs, "a man who hits people", often went with it. The list does not forbid wine (1 Timothy 5:23 recommends a little), but it rules out a man ruled by it. For the long Christian debate on drink, see the topic page on wine.

p: The word appears twice in one chapter: the leader must not be what the false teachers are (1:11).
b: The adjective aischrokerdēs joins "shameful" and "profit." Verse 11 uses the same two words of the false teachers, who teach "for the sake of shameful profit." The repeat is deliberate: the elder is defined against the teachers he must correct. Teachers in the Greek world were often paid, and wandering speakers who sold their teaching were a common target of mockery.

p: An elder's house was where traveling believers stayed, like Zenas and Apollos (3:13).
b: The word philoxenos means "loving strangers." Christians moving between towns, like Zenas and Apollos at the end of this letter (3:13), needed safe places to stay, and a house church's host often became one of its leaders. Paul tells the Romans: "Chase after hospitality to strangers" (Romans 12:13). The same quality is in the overseer list of 1 Timothy 3:2.

t: Sophron: the letter's key word for daily life
p: "Sensible" renders one family of Greek words that runs all through chapter 2.
b: The Greek sōphrōn meant sound-minded, moderate, in control of one's desires. It was one of the four classic virtues of Greek ethics (with wisdom, courage and justice). Titus uses the family six times: the overseer is sōphrōn (1:8), the older men too (2:2), the older women teach the younger ones sōphronizō, "good sense" (2:4), the young women are sōphrōn (2:5), the young men are urged sōphronein (2:6), and grace trains everyone to live sōphronōs, "sensibly" (2:12). The Plain uses "sensible" and "good sense" each time so the reader can follow the thread. Other English Bibles use "self-controlled", "sober" or "discreet".

p: The Greek is a medical word: teaching that is healthy, as opposed to the sick talk of the opponents.
b: The participle hygiainousa means "being healthy" (English "hygiene" comes from the root). The Pastoral Letters speak of "sound" or "healthy" teaching (1 Timothy 1:10; 2 Timothy 4:3; 2:1 here), "sound" words (2:8) and being "sound in the faith" (1:13; 2:2). The picture is of teaching that keeps a body well, set against teaching that spreads like a disease (2 Timothy 2:17). The point is not only correct doctrine but teaching that produces a good life, which is why chapter 2 follows at once.
orig: ἡ διδασκαλία ἡ ὑγιαίνουσα (hē didaskalia hē hygiainousa)

a: correct those who argue against it
p: The verb means to show a person his error. Titus uses it three times.
b: The Greek elenchō means to bring something into the light so that it can be seen to be wrong: to refute, to convict, to correct. The elder must "correct" the opponents (here), Titus must "correct them sharply" (1:13), and he must "correct with full right to command" (2:15). The goal of the correction is stated in 1:13: "so that their faith will be sound." It is meant to heal, not only to win.

t: "Those from the circumcision": who were they?
p: Jewish believers, or teachers of Jewish law. The phrase is the same as in Galatians 2:12.
b: The Greek hoi ek tēs peritomēs means "those of the circumcision." In Acts 11:2 and Galatians 2:12 the same phrase names Jewish believers who pressed for keeping the law ("he was afraid of those from the circumcision", Galatians 2:12). Here it seems to mean teachers among the believers on Crete who taught Jewish "myths" and "commands" (1:14), "genealogies" and "fights about the law" (3:9). Philo, a Jewish writer of the first century, says Crete had Jewish communities (Embassy to Gaius 282), so Jewish believers were likely part of the churches. The verse does not say all Jewish believers were opponents; "especially" names one group among "many." The site's J lens reads the phrase as a dispute inside the church about the law, not as a charge against the Jewish people.
orig: οἱ ἐκ τῆς περιτομῆς (hoi ek tēs peritomēs)

a: talk nonsense and lead minds astray
p: Two rare compound words: mataiologoi, "empty-talkers", and phrenapatai, "mind-deceivers".
b: Mataiologoi are people whose words are empty, "futile" (compare 1 Timothy 1:6). Phrenapatai are "deceivers of the mind", people who cheat others' thinking; the word appears only here in the New Testament, and Galatians 6:3 has the verb: a person who thinks he is somebody "is deceiving his own mind." The false teachers are described by what their talk does: it fills time with nothing and leads people's minds where they should not go.

p: The Greek verb is used for putting a bit or muzzle in an animal's mouth.
b: The verb epistomizō means "stop the mouth", from stoma, "mouth". Paul does not say how. Calvin, who asked how a pastor could silence stubborn people, answered that the word of God refutes them before the church. The verse speaks of answering them, not of force; the elder's tool is to "correct" (1:9).

p: The churches met in houses, so false teaching spread household by household.
b: The early churches met in private homes. A teacher who won over the head of a house could change what a whole group of family members, slaves and dependents heard and believed. The verb anatrepō means "overturn" (2 Timothy 2:18 uses it for upsetting faith). That is why chapter 2 turns to the household: older men, older women, young women, young men and slaves. The letter answers bad teaching in houses with good order in houses.

a: a prophet of their very own
p: Clement of Alexandria and later writers name Epimenides of Crete. Others point to Callimachus. The history is tangled.
b: Paul does not name the poet. Clement of Alexandria (Stromata 1.14), about AD 200, counts Epimenides of Crete among the seven sages and says Paul mentions him in the letter to Titus, but he names no book of Epimenides. In the English of the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Chrysostom says, "It was Epimenides who said this, himself a Cretan"; Koskenniemi notes that Chrysostom names both men, and that the Greek text of the homily gives this line to Callimachus. Athenagoras and Origen quote Callimachus' Hymn to Zeus (third century BC), where the words "Cretans are ever liars" stand in a complaint that the Cretans built a tomb for Zeus, "but thou didst not die, for thou art for ever." Jerome is the first who clearly ascribes a book to Epimenides as the source. Calvin had "no doubt" the speaker was Epimenides and took the line as "a proverbial saying". Koskenniemi argues that the proverb came first, then a logical paradox built on it, and that Epimenides was tied to it only after that. Calling a Greek poet a "prophet" was not odd: Calvin notes that the Greeks sometimes called poets "prophets". For the line in Acts 17:28 that some also ascribe to Epimenides, see the note there.

t: A proverb, an insult, and a puzzle
p: The line is harsh. Readers differ on whom it targets, and later logicians made a paradox of it.
b: Three things to know. (1) The insult was a stock one: Callimachus uses the same words because the Cretans showed a tomb of Zeus, which he took as a lie about a god. (2) If a Cretan says all Cretans are liars, is he lying? Later logicians made this "liar paradox" famous and named it after Epimenides. The letter shows no interest in the puzzle: it says the testimony "is true" (1:13). (3) Whom does it describe? The Greek says "one of them, their own prophet", and "them" may be the teachers of 1:10-11 or the Cretans at large. On the first reading the line is turned against the troublemakers, and the goal is that they be "sound in the faith" (1:13). On the second, the letter accepts the island's bad name. Calvin took it that way: "Nor are these vices charged against one or a few persons, but he condemns the whole nation", though he added that God chose so infamous a nation to receive the gospel early. Chrysostom took the line as aimed at Cretan habits and said Paul used their own writer because "we put them most to confusion when we bring our testimonies ... from their own writers." Readers today also hear an ethnic slur. The Plain leaves "them" as open as the Greek does.

p: Apotomos is from a verb for cutting off. The rebuke is severe, but its goal is healing.
b: The adverb apotomōs comes from apotemnō, "cut off": the correction is to be clean and cutting, not soft. Paul uses the same word in 2 Corinthians 13:10 of his own possible severity. The purpose clause follows at once: "so that their faith will be sound" (healthy). The surgeon cuts to heal.

p: The letter does not say. Guesses range from legends built on the Bible's genealogies to early Gnostic speculation.
b: Titus gives only hints: "Jewish myths", "the commands of people" (1:14), purity rules (1:15), "genealogies" and "fights about the law" (3:9). 1 Timothy 1:4 joins "myths and endless genealogies" too. Readers have proposed: Jewish storytelling that expanded the Bible's lists of ancestors (as in the book of Jubilees); rules about food and purity added to the law; or speculation about chains of heavenly beings, which later Gnostic teachers developed. The letter's own answer is practical: such talk does not produce good works (1:16; 3:9). "The commands of people" echoes Isaiah 29:13, which Jesus quotes against human traditions in Mark 7:7.
r: 1 Timothy 1:4; 1 Timothy 4:7; 2 Timothy 4:4; 3:9; Isaiah 29:13; Mark 7:7; Colossians 2:22

a: All things are clean to those who are clean
p: Like Jesus in Mark 7 and Paul in Romans 14, Titus says what is outside a person does not make him unclean.
b: The opponents seem to have taught rules about clean and unclean food and things. The answer echoes Jesus' teaching that what goes into a person "does not go into his heart", where Mark adds "(With this he made all foods clean.)" (Mark 7:19), and Paul's "All things are clean" (Romans 14:20). The defilement that matters is inside: "their very minds and consciences are stained." Chrysostom put it this way: things are "not clean or unclean from their own nature, but from the disposition of him who partakes of them." The Plain says "clean" (not "pure") so the link with the food passages shows.

p: The conscience, the inner judge, can itself be stained, so that it no longer judges rightly.
b: The Greek syneidēsis, "conscience", is the inner sense that judges right and wrong (Romans 2:15). The Pastorals care much about it: a "good conscience" (1 Timothy 1:5, 19), a conscience "seared" (1 Timothy 4:2). Here both the mind and the conscience are "stained" (miainō, to dye, smear, pollute). The point is grim: those who teach purity rules are themselves impure where it counts, and their inner judge can no longer be trusted.

a: they fail the test for any good work
p: Adokimos is a word for coins or metal that fail the assayer's test.
b: The adjective adokimos means "not approved after testing", like a coin rejected as false. Paul uses it of "a mind that fails the test" (Romans 1:28) and in 2 Corinthians 13:5-7. The verse ends the chapter with the letter's main charge: the opponents claim knowledge of God, but their lives show it is false. The phrase "good work" will come back at the end of each part of the letter (2:7, 14; 3:1, 8, 14).
orig: πρὸς πᾶν ἔργον ἀγαθὸν ἀδόκιμοι (pros pan ergon agathon adokimoi)

a: But you must speak what fits sound teaching
t: A household code for a church in houses
p: Chapter 2 gives duties group by group. Greek writers on the household had a similar pattern.
b: Greek and Roman writers on running a household, from Aristotle on, discussed the relations of husband and wife, father and children, master and slaves. The New Testament has several such lists, called "household codes" (Ephesians 5:21-6:9; Colossians 3:18-4:1; 1 Peter 2:18-3:7). Titus 2 is grouped by age and status instead: older men, older women, young women, young men, slaves. Three times it gives a reason that faces outward: so that God's word is not insulted (2:5), so that opponents have nothing bad to say (2:8), so that slaves make the teaching beautiful (2:10). Readers differ on how far these rules reach today: some treat them as lasting order, others as a strategy for a mission in the Roman world. The cards on this chapter set the churches side by side.

t: Older men, not the office of elder
p: The word here is presbytes, "an old man", not presbyteros, the title of the leaders in 1:5.
b: In 1:5 the leaders are presbyteroi, "elders." Here the word is presbytēs, simply an older man (Luke 1:18; Philemon 9), and in 2:3 presbytis, an older woman. The two words share a root, and the elders of 1:5 would have been drawn from the older men, but 2:2-3 speaks to everyone of that age. Their list echoes the overseer's ("sensible"), so the qualities asked of leaders are asked of all.

p: Paul's usual triad is faith, hope and love. Here endurance takes the place of hope.
b: Paul often groups faith, love and hope (1 Corinthians 13:13; 1 Thessalonians 1:3; 5:8). Titus has faith, love and hypomonē, "endurance", the staying power to hold out under pressure. 1 Timothy 6:11 and 2 Timothy 3:10 list the same three among other virtues. The change suits the older men, who have stood the test of years. Hope has its own place in this letter (1:2; 2:13; 3:7).

a: as people who serve in a holy place
p: One Greek word, hieroprepeis, "suited to what is sacred".
b: The adjective hieroprepēs comes from hieros, "holy, of a temple." The word pictures someone whose bearing fits a sacred place. Many English Bibles flatten it to "reverent", which is the sense, but the Greek image is stronger: the older women carry themselves as if their whole life were holy service. Some readers see a hint that older women had a recognized role in the church, which fits their task of teaching (2:3-4).

p: Diabolos means "slanderer." With the article it is the title "the devil".
b: The noun diabolos means someone who throws accusations, a slanderer. With "the" it is the usual New Testament title for Satan, "the devil" ("the slanderer"). The same plural is used of women in 1 Timothy 3:11 and of people in the last days in 2 Timothy 3:3. In small house churches, gossip could split a community, as Paul's other letters show.

p: Kalodidaskalous: "teachers of good." What and whom did they teach?
b: The word kalodidaskalos, "teacher of what is good", appears only here in the New Testament. Verse 4 says whom they teach: the younger women, in good sense and family life. Some readers take this as a limit (women teach women, in private); others note that the letter gives the older women a recognized teaching role, and that Titus himself is told to teach the young men (2:6-7) but not the young women. Whether this rule sets a pattern for all times is part of the debate on women in ministry; see the card on this chapter and 1 Timothy 2:11-12.

a: teach good sense to the younger women
p: The verb sophronizo means to bring someone to their senses, to train in self-control.
b: Sōphronizō is the verb of the "sensible" family that runs through the chapter (see 1:8). It means to train or call someone to a sound mind, and could be used of correcting. Young wives were often married by family arrangement into a husband's household, so an older woman's guidance was practical help. "Love their husbands" and "love their children" are each one Greek word (philandros, philoteknos).

p: The reason is outward: "so that the word of God is not insulted." Readers weigh it differently.
b: The verb hypotassomai, "submit", is used again of slaves (2:9) and of all believers toward rulers (3:1). In Ephesians the wives' submission stands under the call to all, "submitting yourselves to one another in the fear of Christ" (Ephesians 5:21-22). Here the purpose is stated: "so that the word of God is not insulted." Paul uses the same verb when he quotes Isaiah in Romans 2:24, "The name of God is insulted among the Gentiles because of you." One reading takes the rule as part of a lasting order of the household (see the topic headship); another stresses the reason, as missionary tact in a society that would have heard wives' independence as scandal, which leaves room for different practice where the reason differs. The card on this chapter sets the churches side by side; the card at Ephesians 5 gives their wider teaching on headship.
orig: ὑποτασσομένας τοῖς ἰδίοις ἀνδράσιν (hypotassomenas tois idiois andrasin)

p: The Greek oikourgos means a worker in the house, which in the ancient world meant running a household's work.
b: An ancient household was a workplace: spinning, weaving, food, stores, children, slaves. The woman who ran it was a manager, as the capable wife of Proverbs 31 is. Oikourgos praises a wife who is busy with that work. It does not speak to modern questions of paid work outside the home, which ancient women of most classes also did in markets and family trades (Acts 16:14; 18:2-3). The Byzantine text reads a different word, "keepers at home": see the variant.

t: Typos: the stamp left by a die
p: Titus is to be a typos: a mark, model or pattern others can copy.
b: The Greek typos is the mark left by a blow or a stamp, then a model or pattern. Paul uses it of himself and of churches as examples (Philippians 3:17; 1 Thessalonians 1:7), and 1 Timothy 4:12 tells Timothy the same as here. English "type" comes from it. Titus is to teach the young men by being what he teaches.

p: An opponent inside the church, or a hostile outsider? The phrase allows both.
b: The phrase ho ex enantias is literally "the one from the opposite side." It may be an opponent in the church (the false teachers of 1:10-16), or an outsider watching for a reason to accuse the believers. The pattern of the chapter, with its outward-looking purposes (2:5, 10), suggests outsiders. Either way the strategy is the same: give no grounds for scorn.

a: Slaves should submit in everything to their own masters
p: Many believers were slaves. The letter speaks to them directly, as members of the church.
b: Slavery was everywhere in the Roman world, and many early Christians were slaves in households headed by unbelievers or believers. The text speaks to slaves as people with their own moral choices: they can please, talk back, steal or be trustworthy. It does not tell masters anything, unlike Ephesians 6:9 and Colossians 4:1. Passages like this one were later cited in defense of slavery, and the churches came to judge slavery very differently over time: the cards at Ephesians 6 and Philemon 1:15-16 set out what each church taught and teaches. See also the topic slavery.
r: Ephesians 6:5-9; Colossians 3:22-4:1; 1 Timothy 6:1-2; 1 Peter 2:18-25; Philemon 15-16; 1 Corinthians 7:21

p: The verb nosphizomai is used of Ananias, who "kept back" part of the price (Acts 5:2).
b: The verb nosphizomai means to set aside for oneself, to embezzle. A slave who managed stores or money could easily keep back small amounts. The only other New Testament use is of Ananias: "He kept back some of the money for himself" (Acts 5:2). Instead, believing slaves are to show "good faith", the same word as "faith" (pistis), in its sense of loyalty.

a: make the teaching of God our Savior beautiful
p: The verb kosmeo means to put in order or adorn. The slaves' lives become the teaching's jewelry.
b: The verb kosmeō (from which English "cosmetic" comes) means to arrange or decorate. The surprise is who does the adorning: slaves, the lowest members of the household, make the teaching about God attractive by how they live. The same verb describes women's adornment by good works in 1 Timothy 2:9-10.

p: The verb is epiphaino, the word for a god or ruler showing himself in public. It frames 2:11-14.
b: The verb epephanē, "appeared", and the noun epiphaneia, "appearing" (2:13), were used in the Greek world for a god's visible help and for a ruler's visit; a Syrian king even took the title Epiphanes. Titus speaks of two appearings: grace has already appeared (2:11; in 3:4 God's kindness "appeared"), and believers wait for "the appearing of the glory" (2:13). The first is Christ's coming in history; the second is his coming at the end. The Christian life is lived between them. This is the letter's main way of speaking about Christ; A. Y. Lau's study of it is titled Manifest in Flesh: The Epiphany Christology of the Pastoral Epistles (1996).

p: Does "all people" mean every person, or people of every kind, like the groups just listed?
b: The Greek pasin anthrōpois follows a list of every kind of person: old and young, men and women, slave and free. Some readers take it in that light: grace has appeared for people of every class, even slaves. Others hear a wider claim, that God's saving grace is offered to every human being, as 1 Timothy 2:4 says God wants all people to be saved. The same question is asked of 1 Timothy 2:4 and 4:10, where the churches' readings are set side by side on the election topic.

p: Paideuo means to raise and discipline a child. Grace is pictured as a tutor.
b: The verb paideuō means to bring up a child, to educate and to discipline (Greek paideia, "education"). Here grace is the teacher. That is a striking image in a letter so concerned with rules: good behavior comes from being trained by grace, not from fear of punishment. What grace teaches has two sides: say no ("deny") to ungodliness, and live well in "this present age" while waiting for the next.

a: sensibly, rightly and in a godly way
p: Self-control, justice and piety were standard Greek virtues. Titus fills them with new meaning.
b: The three adverbs, sōphronōs, dikaiōs and eusebōs, name classic Greek virtues: control of oneself, justice toward others, reverence toward God. Some read them as covering the whole of life: oneself, one's neighbor, God. The vocabulary would have been familiar to any educated Cretan, which may be the point: the letter uses the best words of its culture, then ties them to grace, the cross (2:14) and the coming of Christ (2:13).

p: Hope here is not a wish but a sure future: Christ's appearing.
b: In the Bible "hope" is usually the thing hoped for, a sure future that is not yet seen (Romans 8:24-25). The "blessed hope" is the coming of Christ in glory; the "and" that follows likely explains what the hope is. The verb prosdechomai means "wait for" and also "welcome", the word used of those who waited for the kingdom of God (Mark 15:43; Luke 2:25). The Plain's "waiting to welcome" keeps both senses. Some Christians use "the blessed hope" as a name for the rapture; the text itself speaks of an appearing "of the glory".
orig: προσδεχόμενοι τὴν μακαρίαν ἐλπίδα (prosdechomenoi tēn makarian elpida)

p: One article covers "God and Savior", so many read one person, Jesus Christ. Others read two.
b: The Greek is tou megalou theou kai sōtēros hēmōn Iēsou Christou, "of the great God and Savior of us, Jesus Christ." One article ("the") governs both nouns. Granville Sharp argued in 1798 that in such a phrase the two nouns refer to one person, and many scholars and translations read the verse so: Jesus Christ is "our great God and Savior" (so the Berean Standard Bible and the World English Bible). J. Christopher Edwards (2011) calls the two-person reading "the present minority", and argues for it. The King James reading, "the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ", allows two persons, and the New World Translation of the Jehovah's Witnesses reads two: "the great God and of our Savior, Jesus Christ." The chapter page sets out the grammar, the context and the history.
orig: τοῦ μεγάλου θεοῦ καὶ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ

a: He gave himself up on our behalf
p: The phrase echoes Jesus' saying in Mark 10:45 and an early formula Paul uses in Galatians.
b: "Gave himself" is an early way of summing up the cross (Galatians 1:4; 2:20; 1 Timothy 2:6). Behind it lies Jesus' saying that he came "to give his life as a ransom in place of many" (Mark 10:45). The verb "redeem" (lytroō) belongs to the same family as "ransom" (lytron): setting free by paying a price. The topic atonement gives the readings of how the cross saves.

a: redeem us out of every kind of lawlessness
p: Two Old Testament promises to Israel are applied to the church here.
b: The wording follows the Greek Old Testament. In the Septuagint of Psalm 130:8 (129:8 in its numbering) God "will redeem Israel from all its lawless deeds", the same verb and noun as here; this site's Plain of the Hebrew says "from all its guilty deeds" (Psalm 130:8). The Septuagint of Ezekiel 37:23 says God will rescue his people "from all their lawless deeds" and "purify" them, and "they will be my people"; the Plain of the Hebrew reads: "I will purify them. They will become my people, and I will become their God" (Ezekiel 37:23). Both promises were made to Israel. Titus applies them to a church of Jews and Gentiles. Jewish readers note that the promises remain Israel's; Christian readers differ on whether the church shares them, inherits them or replaces Israel. See the topic church and Israel.

p: The Greek periousios is the Septuagint's word for Hebrew segullah, God's special possession.
b: The phrase laos periousios is taken from the Greek Old Testament, where it renders the Hebrew segullah, a king's private treasure. God says at Sinai, "out of all the peoples you will be my own private treasure" (Exodus 19:5), and Deuteronomy repeats it: "to be his people, his own private treasure" (Deuteronomy 7:6; compare Deuteronomy 14:2). This Plain uses the same English so the echo can be heard. In the KJV's English, "a peculiar people" meant a people who were his own, not an odd one. 1 Peter 2:9 applies the same Sinai words to believers.
r: Exodus 19:5; Deuteronomy 7:6; Deuteronomy 14:2; Deuteronomy 26:18; 1 Peter 2:9; Malachi 3:17

a: Let no one brush you aside
p: The verb means to look past someone. Titus' authority came from Paul, not from age or office.
b: The verb periphroneō means "think around", to disregard. Titus was a Greek convert and a delegate, not a local leader, and some on Crete may have resisted him. The letter's public tone ("Grace be with all of you", 3:15, in the plural) suggests it was meant to be read to the churches, so that they would hear Paul's backing for Titus. 1 Timothy 4:12 says the same to Timothy about his youth.

p: Like Romans 13, Titus asks believers to obey the government. Crete was a Roman province.
b: Romans 13:1 opens: "Every person must submit to the authorities above them." Titus uses the same verb and the same word for "authorities" (exousiai), and adds "rulers" (archai); Romans speaks of "rulers" with a different word two verses later (Romans 13:3). Crete was under Roman rule. The command is short and has no explanation, which suggests it was common Christian teaching. The words "rulers and authorities" are used of spiritual powers in Ephesians 3:10 and 6:12, but here they mean human officials. For the long debate on church and state, see the topic and the cards at Romans 13.

p: Epieikes is the virtue of a person who does not insist on every right.
b: The adjective epieikēs describes someone reasonable and yielding, who does not insist on the letter of his rights (Philippians 4:5; James 3:17). Prautēs, "gentleness", is the meekness Jesus praised (Matthew 5:5) and one of the Spirit's fruit ("gentleness", Galatians 5:23). These are to be shown "to everyone", not only to fellow believers.

p: The "we too" puts Paul and Titus among the sinners. The movement from "once" to "but" is common in Paul.
b: The list of vices is not a charge against the Cretans alone (compare 1:12): "we too" includes the writer. The move from what "we" once were to what God did (3:3-4) is a pattern of early Christian teaching: Ephesians 2:1-5 and Colossians 3:7-8 move the same way from the old life to God's act. Its purpose here is practical: believers who remember what they were will be gentle toward outsiders (3:2).

p: The Greek is the word behind English "philanthropy", often praised in kings and gods.
b: Philanthrōpia, "love for human beings", was a virtue Greek writers praised in good kings and in gods who helped mortals. Acts 28:2 uses it for the islanders' kindness to the shipwrecked Paul. Here it describes God himself, joined with chrēstotēs, "kindness" (Romans 2:4; Ephesians 2:7). Like grace in 2:11, God's kindness "appeared" (epephanē): the second epiphany passage of the letter.

a: It was not on the basis of works we ourselves had done in righteousness
p: Titus says what Paul says in Romans and Ephesians: salvation is not earned.
b: The phrase "works ... in righteousness" is not Paul's usual "works of the law" (Romans 3:28), but the point is close to Ephesians 2:8-9: "It is by grace that you have been saved, through faith ... It does not come from works." Readers who see the Pastorals as later note the shift from "law" to good deeds in general; others see a summary of the same teaching for a mostly Gentile church. The letter insists just as firmly on good works as the fruit of salvation (3:8, 14), as Ephesians 2:10 does: "created in Christ Jesus to do good works."

t: Washing of rebirth: what is it?
p: Most readers since the early church see baptism. The churches differ on what the washing does.
b: Loutron is a bath or washing; Ephesians 5:26 uses it of Christ cleansing the church "by the washing of water, with the spoken word." Palingenesia, "new birth, birth again", appears only here and in Matthew 19:28, "when the world is born again." Most interpreters, ancient and modern, see baptism here: Chrysostom says "this purification is called the laver of regeneration", and Calvin, while denying that salvation lies in the water, had "no doubt that he alludes, at least, to baptism." Others read the bath as a picture of the Spirit's inner cleansing, with no reference to the rite. Whether the washing itself gives new birth is one of the great divides; see the card on this chapter.
r: Ephesians 5:26; Matthew 19:28; John 3:5; 1 Peter 3:21; Acts 22:16; 1 Corinthians 6:11

p: Does "by the Holy Spirit" go with both the bath and the renewing, or only with the renewing?
b: The Greek has dia loutrou palingenesias kai anakainōseōs pneumatos hagiou, "through a washing of rebirth and renewal of the Holy Spirit." Grammar allows two readings: one act described twice (a washing that is both rebirth and renewal, done by the Spirit), or two acts (the washing of rebirth, and also the Spirit's renewing). The single "through" is the main argument for one act. Anakainōsis is the word of Romans 12:2, "by the renewing of your mind": renewal is also a lifelong process.

a: God poured out this Spirit on us in rich measure
p: The verb "poured out" is the one from Joel's promise, which Peter quoted at Pentecost.
b: Joel promised, "I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh" (Joel 2:28), and Peter at Pentecost quoted it: "I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh" (Acts 2:17). Titus uses the same verb, ekcheō. The Spirit is poured "through Jesus Christ", as in Acts 2:33. The whole Trinity is in these lines: God our Savior (3:4), the Holy Spirit (3:5), Jesus Christ our Savior (3:6).

a: justified by that grace of his
p: "Justify" here, as in Romans, means to be declared in the right. The order is grace, then heirs.
b: The verb dikaioō, "justify" ("declare to be in the right"), is Paul's key word in Romans and Galatians: "They are justified freely, by his grace" (Romans 3:24). The Greek ekeinou, "of that one", may point to Christ, just named, or to God. Being justified leads to being "heirs", as in Romans 8:17: "If we are children, we are also heirs." The inheritance is "eternal life", which takes the letter back to its first lines (1:2).
orig: δικαιωθέντες τῇ ἐκείνου χάριτι (dikaiōthentes tē ekeinou chariti)

p: The Pastorals mark five sayings this way. Here it seems to point back to 3:4-7.
b: The formula pistos ho logos appears five times in the Pastorals (1 Timothy 1:15; 3:1; 4:9; 2 Timothy 2:11; and here) and nowhere else. It marks a statement as reliable, perhaps a known teaching. Here it seems to point back to 3:4-7, since the verse goes on to "these things": a balanced summary of salvation that some readers think was already used in teaching or worship: God's kindness appeared; he saved us by mercy, not works; through washing and renewal; the Spirit poured out; justified; heirs. The site renders the formula word for word the same in all five places.

p: Proistasthai can mean "be busy with" good works, or "practice" an honest trade.
b: The verb proistēmi usually means to lead or be at the head of something (1 Timothy 3:4-5; 1 Timothy 5:17), but in the middle voice it can mean "apply oneself to, be busy with." So kalōn ergōn proistasthai is most often taken as "devote themselves to good works." A minority, noting 3:14 ("to meet pressing needs"), take it as "practice an honorable trade", that is, earn a living and so help others. The Plain uses "give themselves to" in both 3:8 and 3:14 so the reader sees one phrase.

t: Genealogies and fights about the law
p: The same topics as the "Jewish myths" of 1:14: speculation built on the law and the family lists.
b: The Torah contains long lists of ancestors (Genesis 5; 11; 1 Chronicles 1-9), and Jewish teachers of the period wrote retellings and expansions of these stories, such as Jubilees. "Fights about the law" (machai nomikai) suggests quarrels over how to read the law of Moses. The letter does not refute these teachings point by point; it says they are "useless", because they do not lead to a changed life. 1 Timothy 1:4 makes the same complaint about "myths and endless genealogies".
orig: γενεαλογίαι καὶ μάχαι νομικαί (genealogiai kai machai nomikai)

p: The Greek word gave English "heretic", but here it means someone who creates factions.
b: The adjective hairetikos comes from hairesis, "choice, party, school": the word Acts uses for the "party" of the Pharisees and the Sadducees and even for the Christians (Acts 5:17; 15:5; 24:5). Paul uses haireseis for factions in Corinth and in the list of the works of the flesh (1 Corinthians 11:19; Galatians 5:20). So the hairetikos here is someone who forms a faction and splits the church. The KJV's "heretick" reflects the later meaning, a person who holds false doctrine, which grew from this verse among others. The procedure (two warnings, then separation) resembles Matthew 18:15-17.
r: Acts 5:17; Acts 15:5; Acts 24:5; 1 Corinthians 11:19; Galatians 5:20; Matthew 18:15-17; Romans 16:17

p: Artemas appears only here. Tychicus is Paul's well-known letter carrier from Asia.
b: Artemas is otherwise unknown. Tychicus was "from Asia" (Acts 20:4) and carried Paul's letters (Ephesians 6:21; Colossians 4:7). Paul would send one of them to replace Titus on Crete, so that Titus could come to him. 2 Timothy 4:12 says Tychicus was sent to Ephesus, so perhaps it was Artemas who went to Crete.

p: Several cities had this name. The likely one is in Epirus, on the west coast of Greece.
b: The name means "City of Victory." Several towns were called that; the most likely is Nicopolis in Epirus, in western Greece, founded by Octavian, the later Augustus, to mark his victory at nearby Actium in 31 BC. Dalmatia, where 2 Timothy 4:10 later sends Titus, lies further up the same coast. The note added at the end of later manuscripts says the letter was written "from Nicopolis of Macedonia", which is probably mistaken: the verse says Paul plans to go there, so he had not yet arrived.

t: Zenas the lawyer: Jewish or Roman law?
p: Nomikos means a legal expert. Was Zenas an expert in Moses' law or in Roman law?
b: Nomikos means an expert in law. The Gospels use it for experts in the law of Moses (Luke 10:25), and this site renders it "lawyer" with that meaning there. Zenas, who has a Greek name, may have been such a Jewish expert or a jurist in Roman or local law; the letter does not say. Nothing else is known of him. With Apollos, the learned Jew from Alexandria ("a learned speaker and strong in the Scriptures", Acts 18:24), he seems to be on a journey that passes through Crete, perhaps carrying this letter.

p: The Alexandrian preacher of Acts 18 and 1 Corinthians, still traveling in the church's work.
b: Apollos came to Ephesus from Alexandria and was taught more fully by Priscilla and Aquila (Acts 18:24-28). In Corinth some said "I belong to Apollos" (1 Corinthians 1:12), and Paul wrote, "I planted, Apollos watered, but God made it grow" (1 Corinthians 3:6). Later Paul urged him to visit Corinth again (1 Corinthians 16:12). Here he is traveling once more, and Titus is to see to his needs, in line with the hospitality asked of elders (1:8).

a: so that they will not be without fruit
p: The letter ends as it began: faith that bears good works.
b: The last instruction returns to good works and fruit. Helping travelers like Zenas and Apollos (3:13) is the concrete case. The image of fruit is common in Jesus' teaching (Mark 4:20; John 15:2-8) and in Paul (Colossians 1:10). The false teachers "fail the test for any good work" (1:16); the believers are to be the opposite.

a: Greet those who love us in the faith
p: Many manuscripts add a closing note. The fullest says it was written from Nicopolis to Titus, first overseer in Crete.
b: Many manuscripts, and the KJV after them, add a closing note after 3:15. The shortest form, "To Titus", is in Sinaiticus, Ephraemi, Ψ and 33, and probably in the damaged papyrus P61 (about AD 700). Alexandrinus adds "written from Nicopolis". The Byzantine form reads "The letter of Paul the apostle to Titus, appointed first overseer of the church of the Cretans, written from Nicopolis of Macedonia." These notes are later additions by copyists, not part of the letter. They reflect the tradition that Titus was the first bishop of Crete, which Eusebius also records (Church History 3.4.6).
